newsitem.title: USA: Dlr debuts strong, but wary in US after heady jobs.
newsitem.headline: Dlr debuts strong, but wary in US after heady jobs.

text.p: The dollar began substantially stronger in U.S. trade on Friday, surging to fresh peaks against the mark in the wake of a surprisingly robust U.S. employment report, but retreating thereafter in tandem with bonds.

The key Labor Department release showed a heady 316,000 advance in July payrolls -- much stronger than the 193,000 called for by economists -- and a larger-than-expected decline in the jobless rate to 4.8 percent from 5.0 percent in the prior month.
The report also showed a flat reading $12.23 for average hourly earnings and a decline in the workweek, painting a picture of continued strong growth and well-contained inflation.

"The number by itself is very positive for the dollar ... and we jumped a bit on the back of the report," said Hillel Waxman, chief dealer at Bank Leumi Trust Co of New York. "But people are hesitating."
The dollar opened at 1.8530/34 marks against 1.8375/85 on Thursday, and surged to a 93-month peak of 1.8570 marks after the jobs data, before retreating toward its opening levels.

Against the yen, the greenback opened at 119.00/05, just below its overnight 11-week high of 119.17, and stronger than Thursday's close of 118.60/70. With one eye on a weak bond market, the rate fell below the 119 threshold after the data.
The dollar gained on the Japanese currency in overseas dealings, despite rumors that Japan's Finance Ministry had warned traders not to buy dollars above the 119 level.
Weakness in the Tokyo stock market, shrinking Japanese government bond yields and reports of fund interest underpinned the rate and allowed traders to shrug off the swirling market talk.

The Nikkei 225 suffered its sixth largest drop this year, ending down 527.05 point, or 2.59 percent, at 19,804.38, while the yield on the key 182-issue Japanese government bond fell as low as 2.085 percent against 2.110 on Thursday.
Although some traders were wary of verbal intervention to prop up the yen, many remained sanguine about dollar/yen's prospects given the sharp contrast in fundamentals between the two countries.
"The one thing the G7 has learned ... since the Plaza accord is not to fight market trends," said Stephen Flanagan, vice president at Credit Agricole Indosuez.
"(Verbal intervention) might have an effect on a particular day but it would not be a lasting effect," Flanagan added.

Reinforcing the bullish dollar tone were remarks from Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, who reiterated late Thursday in an interview with Reuters that a strong dollar was in the interests of the United States.
Technicians pegged the next target in dollar/mark at 1.8610 and predicted good interest to sell dollars ahead of 120 yen.
Worries that German officials could manipulate domestic interest rates in an effort to halt the recent run-up in dollar/mark appeared to be fading.
"Given the weekend it's likely to be a volatile session ... but the underlying tone is good and we do see the opportunity for further gains," said Bob Lynch, currency strategist at Paribas.
Dealers said July data from the National Association of Purchasing Management, due at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT on Friday, could help set the tone for the remainder of the day.

In other trade of Friday, sterling was well-bid against the mark, changing hands at a session high of 3.0390 in the mid-morning. Howard Davies, ending his tenure as Bank of England deputy governor, said on Friday that the UK economy may need a modest rise in interest rates.

Sterling was weaker against the dollar, however, opening at $1.6345/55 against $1.6400/07. The dollar began higher at 1.5224/29 Swiss francs against 1.5115/25 on Thursday and slipped to an opening rate of Canadian $1.3773/78 from C$1.3780/85.
The Australian dollar opened at $0.7420/25, down from $0.7475/80 at Thursday's close.
(( -- Noah Barkin, N.A. Forex Unit, 212-859-1673 ))
